title: Sodium-Ion Battery India: Working, vs LFP, Indian Makers
summary: Sodium-ion battery India: how Na-ion cells work, worked e-3W pack vs LFP and NMC, 0 V and cold-weather data, cost, and Indian makers with verified claims.
body_markdown:
A sodium-ion battery is a rechargeable cell that stores energy by moving sodium ions, not lithium ions, between two electrodes. It matters in India because the country imports most of its lithium-ion cells, while sodium comes from salt, which India produces in bulk. The trade-off is energy density: today's Na-ion cells hold less per kilogram and per litre than LFP, so they suit e-3Ws, entry e-2Ws and stationary storage better than long-range cars.


> **In short**
>
>
> - A sodium-ion (Na-ion) cell works like a lithium-ion cell, but it moves sodium ions into a **hard carbon** anode, because graphite stores almost no sodium (2021 Na-ion roadmap, J. Phys. Energy).
> - The best Na-ion cells reach about **175 Wh/kg** , against up to 205 Wh/kg for the latest LFP and 265 Wh/kg for NMC (IEA Global EV Outlook 2026). In our worked 8 kWh e-3W pack, Na-ion is about 8 kg heavier than LFP with the best cells and about 14% bulkier with typical ones.
> - Na-ion cells can be stored and shipped at **0 V** because both electrodes use aluminium foil (Rudola et al. 2021), and the latest cells keep about **90% of capacity at −40 °C** (IEA, Feb 2026).
> - Lithium carbonate fell **86%** between 2022 and 2025, from $63,700 to $9,000 a tonne (USGS). In February 2026 the IEA said lithium is still too cheap for Na-ion to undercut LFP in most uses.
> - Indian activity so far is pilot lines, storage products and company claims: Reliance (Faradion), KPIT with Trentar, Naxion, Rechargion, Macsen Energy (lab results, Oct 2026) and JNCASR research. China holds more than 95% of planned 2030 Na-ion cell capacity (IEA).


This guide covers how the cell works, why it needs a different anode, the three cathode families and a scripted pack comparison against LFP and NMC. It then looks at safety, cold weather, cost, the Indian companies and the jobs. For the two lithium chemistries in depth, see our[LFP vs NMC comparison](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/lfp-vs-nmc-battery) ; this post does not repeat it.


**Courses:** Skill-Lync's[battery technology courses](https://skill-lync.com/courses/battery-technology) cover cell chemistry, pack design, BMS and battery cooling, from short courses to the PG Battery program.


## What is a sodium-ion battery and how does it work?


A sodium-ion battery is a "rocking-chair" cell. On charge, sodium ions (Na⁺) leave the cathode, cross the electrolyte and enter the anode. On discharge they travel back while electrons flow through the external circuit. The cell design, manufacturing steps and most of the equipment are the same as for lithium-ion.


The key hardware difference from lithium-ion is aluminium foil on both electrodes. NaPF₆ is the most widely used salt so far (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021). Drawn by Skill-Lync; script in the run folder.


Three facts about sodium drive most design decisions:


- **It is bigger.** Na⁺ has a radius of 1.02 Å against 0.76 Å for Li⁺, about 34% larger, so it strains the host materials more (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021).
- **It is heavier and gives less voltage.** Sodium weighs 22.99 g/mol against 6.94 for lithium, and its standard potential is −2.71 V against −3.04 V (Ahangari et al. 2025).
- **It does not alloy with aluminium.** Lithium does, so lithium-ion anodes sit on copper foil. Na-ion cells can use lighter, cheaper aluminium on both sides (Bischof et al. 2024).

## Why can't sodium-ion batteries use a graphite anode?


Graphite, the standard lithium-ion anode, stores almost no sodium in conventional electrolytes. Na-ion cells use **hard carbon** instead, a disordered carbon that never turns into graphite however hot it is fired. Practical hard carbons store about 300 mAh/g, close to graphite's 372 mAh/g with lithium (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021).


The reason is binding strength. A 2016 quantum-mechanics study in PNAS found that sodium binds more weakly to almost any host, carbon included, than the other alkali metals do (Liu, Merinov and Goddard 2016). Lithium above it and potassium below it in the periodic table both enter graphite readily.


Think of hard carbon as a house of cards: small curved graphite-like sheets at random angles, with gaps wider than 0.34 nm and closed pores between them. Sodium enters the gaps along a sloping voltage curve from about 1 V to 0.1 V, then fills the pores on a flat plateau below 0.1 V (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021).


The weakness is first-cycle efficiency: below 78% for hard carbon against more than 92% for graphite (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021). More than a fifth of the sodium can be lost into the surface film on the first charge, so designers load extra cathode, which costs energy density.


## Which cathode materials do sodium-ion batteries use?


There are three main families: layered transition-metal oxides, Prussian blue analogues (including Prussian white), and polyanion compounds such as NVPF. Companies have not settled on one; each trades energy, cost, stability and critical-mineral content differently (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021).

One point is easy to miss. Layered oxides, the chemistry closest to mass production, still use nickel and manganese, whose processing is geographically concentrated. Polyanion and Prussian-type cathodes need fewer critical minerals but can still contain vanadium or manganese (IEA, 17 Feb 2026). "Sodium-ion" does not automatically mean "free of critical minerals".


## How much energy does a sodium-ion cell store compared with LFP and NMC?


Less than lithium-ion, but the gap to LFP is narrowing. The IEA puts the latest Na-ion cells at up to about 175 Wh/kg, against up to 205 Wh/kg for the latest LFP and 265 Wh/kg for NMC (Global EV Outlook 2026). It adds that the gap is larger in Wh/L, and volume is what limits vehicle range.

## Worked example: an 8 kWh e-3W pack in sodium-ion, LFP and NMC


For an illustrative 8 kWh electric three-wheeler pack, Na-ion and LFP weigh about the same with typical published cells (59 kg each), but Na-ion needs 14% more volume: 43 L against 38 L. With the best 2026 cells, Na-ion is about 8 kg heavier. NMC811 saves about 24 kg, but LFP packs were more than 40% cheaper per kWh than NMC in 2025 (IEA GEVO 2026).


Cell mass is energy divided by specific energy. To go from cells to a pack, we apply one published benchmark to every chemistry: Frith et al. Here is the catch: those pack factors are a modern cell-to-pack benchmark. A conventional module-based pack fills only 35–40% of its volume with cells (Frith et al. 2023). At that level the Na-ion cells need 69–79 L and the LFP cells 61–69 L. When a pack has to fit under a seat or a floor, those extra litres can decide whether it fits at all.


### The pack-voltage problem


A Na-ion pack swings across a much wider voltage range than an LFP pack of the same nominal voltage. The commercial 18650 cells above are rated from 1.5 V to 4.1 V, 3.0 V nominal (Bischof et al. 2024). With 17 in series for a 51 V class pack, the full window runs from 25.5 V to 69.7 V.


Full rated cell window multiplied by the series count. Real products usually narrow the window in the BMS and give up some capacity. Cell data: Bischof et al. 2024 (Na-ion), Preger et al. 2020 (LFP), LG HG2 datasheet (NMC).


That is a 2.7:1 ratio between highest and lowest voltage, against 1.8:1 for LFP (16 cells, 32.0–57.6 V) and 1.7:1 for NMC (14 cells, 35.0–58.8 V). The motor controller and DC-DC converter must work across it, or the BMS must stop at a higher minimum voltage. There is an upside. Because a layered-oxide Na-ion cell's voltage changes steadily across that window, voltage tells the BMS roughly how much charge is left, which is much harder on LFP's flat curve.


## Are sodium-ion batteries safer than lithium-ion?


Partly. Na-ion cells can be discharged to 0 V and stored or shipped with no energy in them, because the anode sits on aluminium, not copper (Rudola et al. 2021). In thermal runaway, one independent test placed a layered-oxide Na-ion cell between LFP and NMC, closer to LFP (Yue et al. 2024).


A "fully discharged" lithium-ion cell is not really at zero. Push it to 0 V and the copper current collector starts to dissolve, which harms cycle life and safety; that is why rules require lithium-ion cells to ship at 30% charge or less. A Na-ion cell can go to true 0 V, and even slightly negative, without that damage (Rudola et al. 2021). Transport rules now reflect this. IATA's Dangerous Goods Regulations (66th edition, effective 1 January 2025) give sodium-ion batteries their own UN numbers, UN 3551 and UN 3552. They also exempt sodium-ion-powered vehicles whose battery is short-circuited to zero charge (special provision A231).


Here is the catch: Na-ion cells still use a flammable organic electrolyte. In accelerating-rate calorimetry on 18650 cells, the Na-ion cell peaked at 511.7 °C with a maximum heating rate of 2,285.5 °C/min, between the LFP and NCM523 cells. The authors estimate a fully charged cell could self-ignite if stored above 169.6 °C (Yue et al. 2024). "Closer to LFP" is fair; "cannot catch fire" is not. The pack protections in[why EVs catch fire in India](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/why-do-electric-vehicles-catch-on-fire-in-india) still apply.


## Do sodium-ion batteries work better in the cold?


For delivering energy, yes. The IEA reports that the latest Na-ion cells keep around 90% of nominal capacity at −40 °C and can run at up to 70 °C, significantly better than lithium-ion and especially LFP (IEA, Feb 2026). CATL claimed more than 90% at −20 °C for its first-generation cell in July 2021.


Most of India never sees −40 °C, though Ladakh and Himalayan winters come close enough to matter. Heat tolerance may matter more elsewhere in the country, but running without active cooling is still being tested: Sandia lists it as an open question.


Here is the catch: holding capacity in the cold is not the same as *charging* in the cold. Sandia cycled two types of commercial layered-oxide 18650 Na-ion cells at 15 °C. All of them faded fast. Teardowns showed sodium plating, and CT scans of most cells showed cracked jelly rolls (Wittman, Preger et al., SAND2026-23913C, July 2026). Earlier Sandia tests of LFP, NMC811 and NCA cells at 15 °C showed no change or only deformation. It is a preliminary poster on two cell types, but it is a good reason to validate charging limits yourself.


## Is sodium-ion cheaper than lithium-ion?


Not yet, in most uses. On 17 February 2026 the IEA said lithium prices are not high enough for Na-ion to undercut LFP in most applications, though Na-ion is already cost-effective for EVs and storage in very cold climates. The cost case depends mainly on lithium prices and on Na-ion energy density.


Lithium prices drive the Na-ion business case. Source: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (2025 estimated).


When lithium carbonate hit $63,700 a tonne in 2022, sodium looked like an escape route. By 2025 lithium was down to $9,000 and LFP packs averaged $81/kWh (BloombergNEF, Dec 2025), a hard price for a new chemistry to beat. Early-2026 lithium prices were more than twice their level a year earlier, though still about 70% below the 2022 peak, and the IEA notes that big cell makers treat Na-ion capacity as a hedge against another spike.


Na-ion's structural advantages are real: no cobalt, aluminium instead of copper foil, abundant raw materials. In 2021 Faradion put its cell bill of materials 25–30% below an LFP pouch cell (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021), a company estimate from a time of dearer lithium. Scale is the bigger problem today. Na-ion output in 2025 was less than 1% of lithium-ion's (IEA, Feb 2026), and the hard carbon supply chain is small and mostly in China (IEA GEVO 2026).


## Why does sodium-ion matter for India?


India is "mostly dependent on other Asian countries" for lithium-ion batteries, the government told the Lok Sabha on 12 August 2025. As of December 2025, only 1 GWh of the 40 GWh of cell capacity awarded under the PLI scheme for advanced chemistry cells (ACC) was installed. Sodium-ion is attractive as a second chemistry whose main raw material India already has.


- **Demand:** lithium-ion battery demand is projected to rise from 40 GWh in 2025 to about 210 GWh by 2030 (NITI Aayog projection, cited in the Lok Sabha on 16 Dec 2025).
- **Lithium:** world output was about 290,000 tonnes in 2025. India is not among the producers; USGS lists it among countries still exploring lithium deposits. The state-owned KABIL has acquired five lithium brine blocks in Argentina.
- **Sodium:** India produced an estimated 30 million tonnes of salt in 2025, third after China and the United States (USGS 2026).
- **Policy:** the PLI ACC scheme is "technologically agnostic", so Na-ion cells are not excluded by chemistry (Lok Sabha, 16 Dec 2025).


Here is the catch for India. Sodium is abundant, but the sodium-ion *industry* is not spread out. China holds nearly all existing Na-ion cell capacity and more than 95% of the capacity planned for 2030, and the cathode and hard carbon supply chains are just as concentrated (IEA, Feb 2026). Switching to sodium only cuts import dependence if India also makes the cathode powder, the hard carbon and the cells.


## Where does sodium-ion fit, and where doesn't it?


Na-ion fits where cost, safety, cycle life and temperature tolerance matter more than mass and volume. The IEA names small-range cars, urban light commercial vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, forklifts and stationary storage as the best matches (GEVO 2026).


Use Fit Why


Grid, C&I and inverter storage Good Mass and volume matter less; 0 V storage and temperature range help. Indian launches started here.


e-3W, passenger and cargo Good, if it fits Similar mass to LFP in our example, about 14% more volume; daily cycling suits it.


Entry e-2W Possible Small, price-sensitive packs; floorboard volume is the limit.


12/24 V starter batteries Good Replaces lead-acid; CATL claims a 24 V truck battery that starts at −40 °C.


Long-range cars, premium e-2W Poor The IEA estimates an average SUV would reach about 350 km on Na-ion against 400–600 km on lithium-ion.


## Who is making sodium-ion batteries in India?


No Indian company had announced gigawatt-scale Na-ion *cell* production as of 17 November 2026. The activity so far is an acquisition, a licensing deal, pilot lines, packs and storage systems, and research. Performance figures in the right-hand column are the companies' own claims.


Company or lab Confirmed Company claims


Reliance New Energy (Faradion, UK) Agreed to buy Faradion on 31 Dec 2021 (enterprise value £100 million, plus £25 million growth capital); fully owned since 28 Oct 2024. Faradion 2021 data: 160 Wh/kg pouch cells, 3,000 cycles. We found no public confirmation of commercial Na-ion cell output at Jamnagar.


KPIT Technologies (Pune) and Trentar Energy Technology unveiled 12 Dec 2023 with an IISER Pune team; transferred to Trentar on 12 Feb 2025 for upfront fees and royalties over eight years. 100–170 Wh/kg by variant; 80% capacity after 3,000–6,000 cycles; Trentar to invest in 3 GWh of capacity.


Naxion Energy (formerly Sodion, Coimbatore) Launched sodium-ion storage systems (3.5, 5 and 10 kW) for homes and businesses in December 2025. 1.5 GWh a year of pack capacity; a ₹


200 crore, 500 MWh pilot cell plant (2027 target per pv magazine; other reports say end-2026).


Rechargion Energy (Pune, CSIR-NCL spin-off) Pilot plant commissioned in 2024; cells validated by ARAI under IEC 62660 (NITI Aayog case study, 23 Jul 2026). Polyanionic cathode, about 3.7 V, 110–120 Wh/kg, more than 15,000 cycles in testing, tested to −20 °C.


Macsen Energy (Macsen Labs spin-off) Lab results announced 5 Oct 2026; 10,000 m² allocated for a cathode plant and cell pilot line, construction from 2027. Prussian white with hard carbon: 1,500+ cycles, at least 90% capacity after 1,000, more than 150 mAh/g. Third-party verification not disclosed.


JNCASR, Bengaluru (research) Peer-reviewed in *Advanced Materials* (2025): a carbon-coated NASICON anode for fast-charging cells. 80% charge in six minutes and 3,000+ cycles in lab cells (DST, pv magazine, 23 Jun 2025).


The useful question for each row is who tested it. ARAI's validation and the JNCASR paper are outside checks; most cycle counts and energy densities are not, and may come from small lab cells. Until independent large-format data appears, compare them with the 128 Wh/kg that independent testers measured on a commercial 18650.


## What is happening with sodium-ion globally?


China leads. CATL launched its second-generation Naxtra cell on 21 April 2025, rated at 175 Wh/kg, and said in April 2026 that it would reach full-scale mass production by the end of 2026. On 5 February 2026, Changan and CATL unveiled what they call the first mass-production passenger car with Na-ion batteries, due on sale by mid-2026; we could not confirm delivery figures. The IEA also reports that BYD began building its first Na-ion plant in January 2024, LG Energy Solution announced a pilot line in Nanjing, China, and US-based Natron Energy has shut down (IEA, Feb 2026). Na-ion is now an industrial race, and it is being run on supply chains as much as chemistry.


## What engineering jobs and skills does sodium-ion create?


Most Na-ion jobs are lithium-ion jobs plus new chemistry knowledge. The cells are made on similar equipment, packed into similar modules and run by a BMS. Engineers who understand where Na-ion behaves differently are what Indian pilot lines and storage firms need.


Role What changes with Na-ion Skills to build


Cell / materials engineer Hard carbon precursors, Prussian white moisture control, first-cycle loss Electrochemistry, XRD/SEM, coin and pouch cell testing


Electrode process engineer Dry rooms for moisture-sensitive cathodes; aluminium on both electrodes Mixing, coating, calendering, formation


BMS engineer Sloping voltage curve, wide window, 0 V storage, cold-charging limits Cell modelling, SOC/SOH estimation, MATLAB/Simulink


Pack and thermal engineer More volume per kWh; different cooling needs Packaging, thermal and CFD analysis, vibration


Test and validation engineer UN 3551/3552 transport rules; checking company claims IEC 62660 cell tests, abuse testing, data analysis


If you are starting out, learn lithium-ion cell and pack basics first; nearly all of it carries over. Skill-Lync's[battery technology for EVs course using MATLAB and Simulink](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/battery-technology-electric-vehicles-matlab-simulink) covers cell modelling and BMS logic, and the[PG program in battery technology](https://skill-lync.com/mechanical-engineering-courses/masters-certification-program-battery-technology) goes deeper into pack and thermal design. See also[how a battery management system works](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/how-does-a-battery-management-system-bms-work) and, for end of life,[lithium-ion battery recycling in India](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/lithium-ion-battery-recycling-india) .


## Frequently asked questions


### Is sodium-ion better than lithium-ion?


It depends on the job. Na-ion is easier to store and ship, handles cold better and avoids lithium, but it stores less energy per kilogram and per litre: about 175 Wh/kg at best against up to 205 Wh/kg for LFP (IEA 2026). It competes in storage and small vehicles, not yet in long-range cars.


### Are sodium-ion batteries available in India?


In limited form. Naxion Energy launched sodium-ion storage systems in December 2025, and Rechargion has ARAI-validated cells and a pilot plant. As of November 2026, no Indian company had announced gigawatt-scale Na-ion cell production.


### Can a sodium-ion battery replace the LFP pack in my e-scooter?


Not as a direct swap. A Na-ion pack of the same energy is bulkier and has a much wider voltage window, so the charger, motor controller and BMS must be designed for it, and the vehicle must be approved with it.


### How long do sodium-ion batteries last?


Company claims range from 3,000 cycles (Faradion) and 3,000–6,000 (KPIT) to more than 10,000 (CATL Naxtra) and more than 15,000 in testing (Rechargion). Independent long-term data on large cells is still limited, so treat these as claims.


### Why don't sodium-ion batteries use graphite?


Sodium binds too weakly to carbon to form a useful graphite compound, so graphite stores almost no sodium in normal electrolytes. Hard carbon, with wider gaps and closed pores, stores about 300 mAh/g and is the standard Na-ion anode (Tapia-Ruiz et al. 2021; Liu et al. 2016).
